segments: ... and cross-bows {OCR?}.
Frankish kings.
About two hundred men arrived at Mosul by water on the Tigris, by the command of the King of Kings,
so that they might go to Babylon (Baghdad),
prepare ships there, descend to Basra,
and from there to the Persian Gulf (the Red Sea?),
and harm the Egyptians.
Indeed, others of them, about seven hundred men, also went by dry land,
and they remained in Baghdad all winter,
until their purpose was accomplished.
For a story worthy of record happened to the Franks in Baghdad;
and so that the order of our narrative may not be disrupted,
let us return for the present to our subject,
and afterward we will recount {OCR?} the story of these men.
Now when the Kurds heard
that some Franks had arrived in Mosul,
they supposed that they had come on their account,
and they abandoned the fortress and dispersed.
Those who were inside the fortress,
when they were relieved of the Kurds,
wished to go and bring the people of the village of Beth Sayyada {OCR?} to the fortress,
lest they be harmed by the Kurds—
though in truth, if they had left them in their place, they would not have been harmed.
Therefore, these Qayachis, mountaineers, about two hundred horsemen, went down from the fortress
and went to Beth Sayyada,
although they did not care much about these people,
but rather about their own profit.
For as soon as they arrived there,
they even hired out {OCR?} the horses under them to the peasants,
while they themselves came on foot before them.
And so they were scattered from one another like a people without a leader,
until they drew near to the city.
Then certain Kurds who were lying in ambush and watching for them fell upon them,
and although few of them were killed,
they captured many
and plundered everything that was found with them.
Now the bandits who were in Syria,
when they heard that the Kurds had besieged the fortress of Erbil,
supposed that as soon as they subdued it, they would plunder, kill, take captives, and carry them off to Syria.
So there gathered together from then on about two thousand men,
and they came to the assistance of the Kurds.
And when they arrived, they did not find them as they had supposed;
moreover, they themselves were not able to approach the fortress, because of the strength and warlike prowess of those inside.
